name: Republicanism
summary: Republicanism holds that a political community is the common thing of its people and should be governed by law, not by the arbitrary will of any person. Its central value is freedom as non-domination, secured through consent of the governed, mixed or separated powers, accountable and contestable office, and civic virtue among citizens. It opposes hereditary and personal rule, and is split on questions of social policy, the economy and religion that the tradition did not settle.
scope: Civic republicanism as a tradition running from Cicero, Machiavelli and Harrington through the American founders (Federalist No. 51) to the neo-Roman theory of Skinner and Pettit. It covers modern French republicanism only where noted (secularism, uniform law). It excludes republican parties and anti-monarchist movements as organizations. Many social and economic statements were not addressed by the tradition and are low-confidence inferences or 0.

furtherReading.note: Careful account of freedom as non-domination and contestatory democracy.

furtherReading.note: Madison's case for checks and balances in a republic.

furtherReading.title: Republicanism (Wikipedia)

keyFigures.name: Philip Pettit
keyFigures.role: Developed the contemporary theory of freedom as non-domination and contestatory democracy.

keyFigures.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
keyFigures.role: Central thinker of the classical republican tradition in the Renaissance.

keyFigures.name: James Harrington
keyFigures.role: Source of the republican ideal of an empire of laws and not of men.

sources.title: Republicanism
sources.author: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.usedFor: Non-domination, rule of law, civic virtue, contestatory democracy, welfare, unions, basic income, militarism.

sources.title: Republicanism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Opposition to monarchy, popular sovereignty, mixed government, church-state, standing armies, property, imperialism.

sources.title: The Federalist Papers: No. 51
sources.author: James Madison or Alexander Hamilton (Publius), 1788
sources.usedFor: Separation of powers, ambition checking ambition, federalism, minority rights, justice as end of government.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Contemporary republicans (Pettit and others) worry that low-paid workers are dominated by employers and support protections such as stronger unions and income floors.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Markets are not seen as inherently dominating, but republicans do not hold that they outperform government; the state must correct dependence they produce.

public-ownership.rationale: Republicans favor widely dispersed property and checks on power; concentrated state ownership is not a republican program, though not excluded.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Severe inequality exposes the poor to domination, so republicans accept redistribution, and the classical tradition feared concentrated wealth corrupting the republic.

unions-good.rationale: The SEP entry lists stronger unions as a republican remedy for employer domination.

property-fundamental.rationale: Classical republicans tied independent citizenship to property, yet accepted public limits on it; Pocock notes property was seen as perpetually threatened by corruption.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Republicans want private power held accountable and contestable, which supports regulating large firms; the SEP cites workplace democracy and legal checks on employers.

cut-welfare.rationale: The state must provide for basic needs to prevent exploitative dependence, so cutting welfare is opposed; the dependency argument is not the republican one.

worker-ownership.rationale: Workplace democracy is discussed by republicans, but collective worker ownership is not a defining republican demand.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Republicans fear unchecked, unaccountable state power and demand contestability of officials' decisions, so open-ended surveillance is viewed with suspicion.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Republicans are split between protecting free public contestation and protecting equal standing of citizens; the texts do not settle it.

strong-leader.rationale: Republicans oppose personal rule and unchecked executive power: an "empire of laws and not of men", and ambition must be made to check ambition.

state-harmful.rationale: Republicans see law and the state as what makes freedom possible; without them people are ruled by the stronger.

limit-guns.rationale: Classical republicans praised the citizen militia and distrusted standing armies, while modern republicans differ on gun regulation.

empower-police-military.rationale: Standing armies were viewed as a source of corruption and a threat to liberty, so republicans prefer militias and checks on armed forces.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: The tradition says little; republicans split on whether it involves domination or consent.

decide-locally.rationale: Federalism and divided power are endorsed republican devices, and early modern republicanism fit small self-governing communities, though national republics also exist.

traditional-family.rationale: Not a republican question; classical writers valued household and civic virtue but modern republicans vary.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Equal standing under the law is central, and contemporary republicans generally treat exclusion from civil institutions as a status inequality, but the tradition did not address it.

more-religion-public.rationale: French and modern republicanism pursue secular public institutions (Ferry laws), though Cromwell's Commonwealth was a Christian republic.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Republicans see domination of groups as a wrong the state should remedy, though French republicanism favors color-blind law, which critics say perpetuates discrimination.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Republicans value civic culture and public spirit but this is not framed as preserving national tradition.

gradual-change.rationale: Republicans prize established constitutional order and also revolutions against tyranny (Paine, Wolfe Tone), so the tradition is split.

reduce-immigration.rationale: No republican position; civic membership is defined by law and participation, not origin.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Global republican theory exists (Pettit on international order) but no stated majority view; republics historically prize self-rule.

nation-first.rationale: Republicans value self-government for the polity but do not prescribe nationalism; Milton's international republicanism is cosmopolitan in part.

revolution-justified.rationale: The tradition justifies overthrowing tyranny, and republics emerged from revolutions in America, France and Ireland.

experts-over-public.rationale: Republicans want public contestation and accountability of officials; discretionary power is acceptable only if it answers to public goals.

central-planning.rationale: Republicans favor dispersed power and accountability; a planned economy concentrates power, though the texts do not address it.

basic-income.rationale: The SEP entry names basic income among republican proposals for securing independence from dependence.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The classical ideal ties independent citizenship to property, and republicans fear dependence and concentrated power.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Republicans accept markets and wage labor, seeking to prevent exploitative dependence rather than abolish them.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Republicans favor contestable public decisions over state-recognized bodies setting wages and prices, though they support unions.

one-party-rule.rationale: Rule by one party above contestation contradicts contestatory democracy and checks on power.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Most republicans reject hereditary rule, though some English thinkers accepted a monarchy constrained by law.

democracy-best.rationale: Modern republicanism rests on popular sovereignty, but classical republicans favored mixed government and feared majority tyranny, hence not +2.

direct-votes.rationale: Republican institutions are overwhelmingly representative; Madison argues a republic checks majority factions through representation and size.

workers-councils.rationale: Not a republican institution; republics rest on parliaments and constitutions.

natural-rulers.rationale: Republicanism is defined against hereditary and personal rule, with officials seen as corruptible and requiring checks.

political-violence-never.rationale: The tradition justifies resisting tyranny and defending the republic by arms through militias.

war-builds-character.rationale: Classical republicans praised martial virtue, but Sidney and Milton rejected conquest; the position is split.

separate-church-state.rationale: Modern republicanism, especially French, separates church and state in public institutions, though Cromwell's republic was Christian.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The republic is the people's common agreement on law; scriptural law is not the republican basis, despite the Christian Commonwealth.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Law and public armed forces are public things (res publica) and republicans fear private power and dependence.

military-superiority.rationale: Roman republicans valued strength but later republicans distrusted standing armies; no settled position.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Republicans stress shared civic institutions and the common good over class conflict, though Machiavelli saw conflict between classes as productive.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Republicans want equal standing and independence for all, not equal outcomes.

civilizational-union.rationale: Republicans organize around the self-governing polity, not civilizational blocs.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The tradition stresses civic virtue and public spirit over private interest, though Madison designs institutions that harness ambition.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Classical republicanism stresses civic duty and virtue, while modern republicans entrench rights; the tradition is split.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Republicans want officials answerable to citizens through reasoned contestation, which opaque algorithmic rule would hinder.

restore-past-order.rationale: Republicanism does value Roman and classical models but as a standard for present self-government, not a restoration of an order.

direct-action.rationale: Republicans channel change through constitutional institutions and public contestation.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Republicanism is a theory of political community under law, incompatible with abandoning it.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Republicans secure basic needs for independence but do not hold distribution by need as a general principle.

production-for-use.rationale: Republicans accept markets so long as they do not dominate.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Republicans worry about employer domination but do not hold that profit is itself exploitation.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Rule by one class over others without contestation is opposed to republican law and checks.

collective-farming.rationale: Republican ideals favor independent property-holders, not collectives.

taxation-theft.rationale: Republicans treat public revenue and law as what sustains a free commonwealth.

harm-principle.rationale: Republicans defend freedom as non-domination and accept restrictions on arbitrary power, not the liberal harm principle.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Republicans entrench individual rights but also value collective self-rule and the common good.

conscription.rationale: Classical republics relied on citizen militias and many accepted civic military duty, while modern republicans differ.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Republicans place freedom in citizens' ability to participate and contest, so voice is central.

state-as-business.rationale: The republic is the people's common thing, not a firm, and officials owe public accountability.

positive-liberty.rationale: Republican freedom is non-domination, which is neither pure non-interference nor material capacity, though it entails material independence.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Republican citizenship rests on equal civic standing, and the claim of natural inequality is opposed.

organic-representation.rationale: Republicans favor elected representation of citizens, not family or corporate bodies.

total-state.rationale: A state directing all life is the opposite of a limited constitutional republic. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

national-rebirth.rationale: Machiavelli speaks of returning republics to first principles, but this is not a fascist-style rebirth.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Classical republicans praised Roman expansion but modern republicans such as Milton and Sidney opposed imperialism.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Authority resting on personal loyalty is the personal dependence republicans oppose. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

bound-labor.rationale: Legally bound labor is domination, the thing republicanism opposes. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Republicans are not associated with this claim.

universal-morality.rationale: Cicero, a founding republican, appealed to natural law, but modern republicans do not all share this.

single-common-good.rationale: Classical republicans stress the common good, while Madison builds a republic around balancing competing interests; the tradition is split.

workplace-democracy.rationale: The SEP entry lists workplace democracy among republican measures against dominating employers.

school-vouchers.rationale: French republicanism treats public schooling as a civic institution; vouchers are not a republican proposal.

economic-freedom.rationale: Republicans link liberty to material independence but not to free-market economics.

rule-by-example.rationale: Republicans rely on law and institutional checks rather than the virtue of rulers: "if men were angels, no government would be necessary".

reason-over-faith.rationale: Republicans emphasize public reason-giving but do not demand reason as the only guide.

class-collaboration.rationale: Republicans prefer a common civic framework but accept conflict as productive.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Republicans venerate classical heritage and civic education.

workers-nation.rationale: The republican tradition never addressed this question and no principle clearly settles it.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Classical republics excluded women, but modern republicans hold equal standing; not explicit in sources.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Equal civic standing is opposed to legal racial classification.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The republic is the common thing of the people, not a ruling-class instrument.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: French republicanism expects civic assimilation but others allow pluralism.

national-mission.rationale: Founding American republicans hold such a view, others reject it; Milton opposed imperialism.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Republicans identify structural domination, and feminist republicans apply it to gender, but this is not core.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Officials are corruptible rather than inherently corrupt, so institutions must check them.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Equal standing and bodily rights are not compatible with coercive eugenics.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Republicans require accountability of all public power and contestation of its decisions.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The republican state secures basic needs and independence beyond a minimal state.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: French republican principle holds one civil law for all citizens regardless of religion.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Not a republican position; the United Irishmen sought to remove religious disqualifications.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: French republicanism removed church influence from state schools through Ferry laws.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Popular sovereignty and government resting on the people are the core of republicanism.

population-transfer.rationale: Republican equal citizenship opposes expelling minorities.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Republicans accept lawful coercion by public authority.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Republicans split between pluralism and defending the republic against subversion.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Freedom as non-domination, defined as having no one with the capacity to interfere arbitrarily, is the central republican value.

separated-powers.rationale: Separated and mixed powers are classical republican devices that Federalist No. 51 defends: ambition must counteract ambition.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Republicans want widespread property but the tradition does not address public housing sales.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Classical republics used lots for some offices, but later republicans such as Madison favored election, so adherents split.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Republicans accept rare constitutional emergency powers (the Roman dictatorship) but hold that arbitrary power is domination and law must bind rulers.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: The tradition does not address price ceilings, and republicans split on market intervention.

party-controls-media.rationale: Republicans demand accountable, contestable government and free public debate, so government control of the press is the arbitrary power they reject.

party-commands-army.rationale: Republicans distrust standing armies and put the military under civilian, constitutional authority, never a party.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Republican writers prize civic virtue, which could support a residency period, but the tradition sets no length.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Classical republics often left office unpaid or modestly paid to guard against corruption, but the tradition has no settled rule on pay levels.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The tradition locates sovereignty in the people and has produced both confederal and national republics, so adherents split on pooling it.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Mixed government and separated powers aim to prevent any one person holding unchecked command, as Federalist No. 51 argues.

clerical-rule.rationale: Freedom as non-domination and rule by the consent of the governed are incompatible with final authority resting in a clerical class.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Civic virtue led some republicans (Machiavelli, Rousseau) to favor moral supervision of culture while liberal-leaning ones opposed it, so it is split.

recall-officials.rationale: Republicans want office to be accountable and contestable, which supports ways for citizens to remove officials who lose their confidence.

people-in-arms.rationale: The SEP and Wikipedia describe the tradition's preference for citizen militias over standing armies as a guard against domination.

minority-language-support.rationale: The scope notes that modern French republicanism stresses uniform law and a single civic language, which cuts against special support for minority languages.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The scope notes that French republicanism stresses uniform law and equal treatment, which cuts against group exemptions from general laws.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: The tradition did not address sovereign debt, and non-domination could be read to favour either relief or repayment; adherents split.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Neo-Roman theorists treat private economic power as a source of domination, but classical republicans prized independence as such; split.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Republicanism rests on popular sovereignty, so a constitution is properly founded by the people through an elected body.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Freedom as non-domination is the central value, and arbitrary power over citizens is what republicans oppose.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Republicans favour accountable office but accept elected, appointed or indirectly chosen heads; the tradition has no settled view.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Independent institutions can serve non-domination if contestable, but unaccountable power troubles republicans; adherents split.

collective-defense.rationale: The tradition did not settle alliances; the founders warned against entanglements while modern republics join defense pacts.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Republicanism has historically subordinated religious institutions to civil authority, most strongly in French republicanism.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Republics divide: some, as in the American system, make the head of state a partisan executive, while parliamentary republics use a ceremonial president.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Federalist writers defended the Union, yet the tradition rests on consent of the governed; adherents split.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Federalist No. 51 defends division of power between federal and state governments, which allows regional self-government.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Republicanism opposes hereditary and personal rule and rests on popular sovereignty, which excludes sacred rulers.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Rule by law and not by persons, with no one above the law, is the core of republican freedom as non-domination.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Mixed government balancing the few and the many is a classical republican ideal from Polybius and Cicero to Harrington.

leader-cult.rationale: Glorifying a leader invites domination and corrupts civic virtue, which republicans oppose.

no-bailouts.rationale: The tradition did not address bailouts and adherents are split.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Federalist No. 51 and mixed government aim to guard rights against majority faction, so republicans accept constraints on majorities.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: The tradition did not address gender quotas; adherents are split.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Republicanism opposes hereditary and personal rule and holds that no one should rule by birth.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Republicanism treats rule over others without their consent as domination, and the SEP and Wikipedia describe republican opposition to imperialism.

patriotic-education.rationale: Civic republicans hold that free government depends on citizens' civic virtue and attachment to the common good, which schooling is meant to cultivate, though the stress falls on civic duty over flag pride.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: The tradition never addressed it; equal standing under law pulls toward colorblind rules while concern for domination of disadvantaged groups pulls toward remedies, so adherents split.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Republicans favor constitutional limits on power and protection of minorities from majorities, as Federalist No. 51 argues, though some strands trust popular contestation over judicial entrenchment.

elective-rulers.rationale: Republicanism opposes hereditary and personal rule; office is held by choice of the people and accountable.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Neo-Roman republicanism holds that rule outside the law is domination and that consent of the governed is the basis of government.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Republicanism has government by law and consent of the governed, with representative assemblies, though it divides powers and does not make any one body supreme.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Civic republicanism holds that freedom and the good life depend on active citizen participation in public affairs.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: The tradition focuses on law and institutions but does not give a theory of cultural hegemony.

native-born-offices.rationale: Republican sources do not agree on citizenship criteria; adherents are split.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Republicans are split between civic memory and rejection of domination; no common position.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Montesquieu's republicans linked institutions to circumstances while others held them as universal; split.

filial-duty.rationale: The tradition values civic virtue and family piety in Rome but did not settle family obligations; adherents are split.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: The tradition did not address foreign investment; adherents are split between protecting the community and open markets.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: The tradition did not address pension design; adherents are split.

single-official-language.rationale: French republicans favour a single common language while Anglo-American republicans do not; adherents are split.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: The tradition did not address foreign land ownership; adherents are split.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: The tradition did not address covert proxy warfare; adherents are split between self-government principles and national interest.

corporate-influence.rationale: Republican theory treats corruption by private factions and wealth as a threat to non-domination and the common good, and favours curbing their sway over office.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Population policy was not a concern of the republican theory this audit draws on, and adherents are split.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Republican accountability and contestability require open records so citizens can challenge those in office; Federalist No. 51 stresses citizen control of government.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Republican tradition values the sovereignty of the self-governing people, but Pettit also extends non-domination to international order, so adherents split.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Republican theory has no settled position on regional fiscal transfers: civic solidarity favours pooling, while federalism favours local control, as in Federalist No. 51's divided powers.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Neo-Roman republicans want property widely held and protected from domination, but do not teach a division between personal and productive property.

defeat-communism.rationale: Republicanism arose before communism and says little on it; republicans oppose arbitrary rule but split on whether to coexist or confront it.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: The tradition cares that services protect citizens from dependence, but has no stated view on who delivers them, so adherents are split.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Republicanism did not settle a view of capitalism's historical role: Pettit stresses its risks of domination, while earlier republicans praised commerce, so it is split.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Republicans stress freedom from domination, including in the household and workplace, which opens room for economic reform, but the tradition has no settled view on whether it is required.

socialized-care.rationale: Republican domination analysis targets unequal household relations but does not endorse public housework services; adherents are split.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Republican traditions value free public discourse and rule by law; French republicanism has promoted the national language, but purging loanwords is not a republican principle.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Republicans do not frame their politics as a third way between capitalism and communism, and range from market to socialist; adherents are split.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Contestatory democracy and rule of law require accountable government and the freedom to oppose it.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Republicans favour a separation of church and state and oppose imposing religion.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Republican theory is critical of imperialism and of rule over others without their consent.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Popular sovereignty and consent, not religious law, ground legitimacy, though armed removal is reserved for tyranny.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Civic virtue and contestatory democracy call for active citizen participation.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: The tradition did not address overlapping oppressions; adherents are split.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Republicans do not treat left and right as obsolete; split.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Republicanism holds that authority comes from the people's consent, not from God or a hereditary ruler.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Republicans distrust standing armies but favour citizen militias, not abolition.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Republicanism opposes hereditary and personal rule; office is held by the people's grant and not passed on to children.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: The tradition did not address credit institutions; republicans differ on economic organisation, so this is left neutral.

property-franchise.rationale: Classical republicans such as Harrington and many American founders tied citizenship to independent property; modern republicans reject this, so the answer is guarded.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Non-domination between persons is central, but linking women and nature is an ecofeminist claim outside the republican tradition.

reification.rationale: Republicanism critiques domination by persons and arbitrary power, not capitalism's relations in this Marxian sense.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Government by law, not by the arbitrary will of any person, is the core of republican freedom and the rule of law.

racial-franchise.rationale: Republicanism's ideal is a community of free and equal citizens governed by law; limiting rights to one racial group is domination of the excluded, though historical republics did so.

open-government-data.rationale: Republican accountability and contestability of office require that citizens can see and challenge public decisions.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Republican civic virtue and equal citizenship are at odds with targeting fellow citizens for their religion.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Republican writers from Harrington to Rousseau worried that great wealth lets some dominate others, and the SEP notes republican concern for limiting the inequalities that create dependence.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Republicans want the state to secure basic needs so that no one depends on another's goodwill, which charity alone cannot do.

rent-control.rationale: The tradition never addressed housing; non-domination might justify limits on landlords' power over tenants, but republicans also defend property, so adherents split.

abolish-ip.rationale: Classical republicans did not discuss intellectual property and modern republicans are divided; nothing in non-domination settles it.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Republican virtue honours labor and fears dependence, but the tradition defended property ownership as the basis of independence, so it is split.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Republics honored citizens who died for the common good, but modern civic republicans resist calling them saints; the religious framing is not part of the tradition, so adherents are split.

god-not-male.rationale: Republicanism, as a political theory, is indifferent to how God is described; religious views among republicans vary.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Republicanism offers no theory of religious texts; its secular strand leans against such tests while others are indifferent, so it is split.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Republicans hold that all citizens share equally in the common thing and that no group may dominate another, so reserving economic life for a national majority contradicts non-domination.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: The tradition did not define socialism, and republicans split on economic systems, so there is no settled answer.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Republicans are divided on public versus private provision; the tradition mostly concerns political office, so adherents split.

second-chamber.rationale: Mixed government and dividing the legislature into branches are classical republican devices, and Federalist No. 51 recommends a divided legislature.

family-wage.rationale: The tradition did not address wage-setting; adherents split between civic-minded support and market views.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Civic virtue is central but the tradition is split between secular and religious strands, and French republicanism stresses secularism.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Republicans from Machiavelli on valued citizen armies and sometimes expansion, while the founders stressed defence, so adherents split.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Republicanism has no settled view on environmental instruments and adherents could favor taxes, regulation or public investment.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: The tradition did not address legal borrowing limits; republicans split between sound-finance and activist views.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: The tradition did not set an economic blueprint, and contemporary republicans differ on how far to go.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Republicanism is a theory of liberty and government, not of religion; it is indifferent, and its secular strand leans against such claims.

farm-price-support.rationale: The tradition never addressed farm support; Roman and later republicans valued independent small farmers but views on state aid are split.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Republicanism has no stated view on language naming; French republicanism favours one national language but the tradition as a whole is split.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Republicanism rests on popular sovereignty and rejects inherited or customary rule, so hereditary authorities have no formal lawmaking place.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Civic virtue and the common good can justify limits on liberty, but republicans also defend liberty strongly; the tradition is silent.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: French republicanism expects assimilation to a shared civic language, but the wider tradition did not address it and is split.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Unions are not central to the tradition; s1 notes some modern republicans support them as protection against domination, but classical republicans are silent.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: The tradition separates church and state and opposes establishment (s2), which French republican laicite carries furthest.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Republicanism holds freedom as non-domination, requiring rule of law, civic virtue and contestation, so elections alone do not make a government legitimate (s1).

negative-income-tax.rationale: Basic-income schemes are discussed by Pettit as a means of securing independence (s1), but there is no republican line on a negative income tax.

indirect-election.rationale: Republicans are split: the Federalist set up indirect selection for some offices, while others stress direct contestation.

national-church-status.rationale: The tradition opposes established religion and favours separation of church and state, as in French secular republicanism.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Republicans hold that no one may wield arbitrary power, and the rule of law and due process are the safeguard against it, which excludes killing without trial.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Republicans accept public limits on property and hold no settled view on compensation for resource appropriation; adherents are split.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Republicans favour mixed government, contestable office and checks on personal power, and the SEP describes parties and groups as part of the contestatory structure, so bypassing them for a leader is opposed.

national-resource-control.rationale: The tradition did not address resource ownership against foreign control, and republican strands differ on it.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: The tradition did not address financial taxation, and republicans are split on economic policy.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: The tradition did not address this question, and modern republicans are split on it.

multipolar-world.rationale: The tradition did not address world order, though Pettit's international theory opposes domination between states; adherents are split.

material-over-identity.rationale: The tradition did not address left strategy, and republican writers are split on it.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Republicanism opposes arbitrary rule and requires contestable, accountable office, which a permanent single-party leadership denies.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The state must provide for basic needs to prevent exploitative dependence, so cutting welfare is opposed; the dependency argument is not the republican one. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: A person is not free if someone else has the power to interfere in their life arbitrarily, even if that power is never used.
missingStatements.rationale: This is the republican definition of liberty as non-domination, set out by Pettit and Skinner.

missingStatements.text: Political power should be divided among separate bodies that check one another.
missingStatements.rationale: Separation of powers and mixed government are classical republican devices that the SEP says contemporary republicans still endorse, and Federalist No. 51 argues that ambition must counteract ambition.

notes: Classical and modern strands differ: Roman and Renaissance writers favored mixed government and martial virtue, while modern republicanism often means popular sovereignty and an elected head of state. French republicanism is more secular and uniform than Anglo-American. Many answers rest on principle rather than stated position.
